Keep a rule-change log and measure what share of changes followed a documented test on N or more trades versus a short losing run.
Measure the R of trades taken after a daily loss limit would have ended the session.
gaps: No KB note covers versioning a method: when a rule change is justified, how it is tested and how the old version is retired.
Links between emotion tags and outcomes rest on T4 practitioner heuristics with no data in the KB.
Prospect theory and the disposition effect are cited only through summaries; the underlying papers have no node in the allowed index.

nodes.summary: Starting from 'how much can I make?' distorts judgment and makes every move look like an opportunity. The trader first asks about understanding, evidence, model fit, probabilities, the cost of being wrong, reward against risk and consistency with the process, and only then considers the money, accepting missed moves without abandoning discipline.

grounded_in.why: FOMO and greed, listed in the note, are how the pursuit of money makes every movement look like an opportunity.
Planning the trade and trading the plan puts the established process ahead of the trade's payoff.
Money is evaluated through expected value per trade after the decision questions are answered, not as a target in itself.
Expressing outcomes in R rather than dollars turns 'is the potential return sufficient to justify the risk?' into a ratio instead of a wish.
The note observes that profit targets encourage over-aggression near deadlines, a direct example of money objectives distorting decisions.
Process over outcome, as the note frames Duke and Douglas, is the probabilistic basis for following decisions rather than P&L.

supported_by.why: Tharp moves attention from dollars to R-multiples and expectancy, so performance is judged by the quality of the system rather than the money made.
Duke's process-over-outcome stance supports answering the decision questions before looking at the payoff.
Livermore's lesson that tips and hope are poison records repeated losses from trading on desire rather than on conditions.
Douglas's consistency principles (identify edges objectively, predefine and accept risk) put the process ahead of the money.
The KB's synthesis finds the wizards share risk control and discipline rather than any money-making method.

challenged_by.why: Its risk section backtests the evaluation pass rate under a firm's real rules and prices each funded account (a worked $100 / 25% = $400 example), showing the money structure can legitimately define the objective a process is built for.
Gunther's axiom to always bet meaningfully argues that a speculator who keeps money out of the decision will not stake enough for good decisions to matter.

operationalized_by.why: Its foundational principles state that the goal is a repeatable process, not a dollar figure, with money as a by-product.
Rule 11 sets targets at liquidity pools and never from dollar goals or arbitrary point counts.
Rule 13 hides the running P&L during the trade and rule 17 grades the process rather than the P&L.
Rule 1 puts mindset first: emotional stability, accepting that not every day is a trading day, and learning ahead of quick money.
Rule 5 asks for motivation from goals, growth and mastery rather than money alone, and sets one process goal per session.
Its ten gates (edge, regime, session, bias, location, trigger, invalidation, R:R, size, state of mind) contain no money target, and size is derived from equity x risk% / stop.

measurable_as: Add a journal field recording whether a trade was prompted by the plan or by a P&L goal (a daily target, recovering a loss), and compare expectancy.
Measure how trade frequency and size change as the account approaches a daily profit goal or a prop-firm profit target.
Compare the R of trades tagged as chasing a missed move with planned entries.
Record whether all seven Section XIII questions were answered before entry and test the completion rate against outcomes.
gaps: No KB data shows how P&L visibility or profit targets change behaviour; hiding P&L is an untested practitioner heuristic.
No concept note on goal setting or incentive design; profit-target effects appear only in the prop-firm note.
The KB does not define what 'profitability' should mean as an objective (growth rate, drawdown-constrained return), beyond the Kelly growth criterion.

nodes.summary: Capital is the resource that buys future participation. Because even a positive-expectancy strategy meets unfavourable sequences, sizing, leverage, drawdowns and ruin must be managed so that being wrong never removes the ability to continue; losses are asymmetric, since a 50% loss needs a 100% gain to recover.

grounded_in.why: The note gives the recovery formula 1/(1-DD) - 1 behind Section XIV's 50% to 100% example, plus streak damage under fixed-fractional risk and the gambler's-ruin approximation.
Fixed-fractional and volatility-unit sizing are the mechanisms that keep a sequence of losses survivable.
Betting more than twice Kelly gives negative growth even with an edge, the formal reason over-sizing destroys future participation.
The note calls leverage the root cause of most blown accounts and insists that risk is set by stop distance x size, not by available leverage.
Correlated positions compound risk invisibly and correlations rise toward 1 in crises, so per-trade limits alone do not protect capital.
Trailing drawdowns and daily loss limits make survival path-dependent, the clearest real-world case of capital as the licence to keep trading.
Sizing inversely to volatility keeps the money at risk constant when markets become wilder.

supported_by.why: Vince shows that leverage drives both growth and ruin, the trade-off behind Section XIV.
Tharp's sizing strategies and R-multiple simulations are built to reach objectives while surviving drawdowns.
The collected theory of growth-optimal betting, including fractional Kelly, formalises sizing for long-run growth and survival.
LTCM's collapse shows leverage, correlation and liquidity risk overwhelming a strong model, the failure Section XIV is written to prevent.
Taleb argues rare, high-impact events dominate outcomes and are underestimated, so sizing must allow for sequences worse than history shows.
Hite's risk-first rule of never risking more than 1% on a trade is the practitioner form of capital preservation.
Feller's classic treatment of ruin problems is the mathematical source of probability-of-ruin reasoning.
Jones's defence-first stance puts protecting capital ahead of prediction.

challenged_by.why: Druckenmiller argues for heavy concentration when conviction is high, recalling Soros taking the 1992 sterling short to 200% exposure, so maximal preservation can forgo the rare outsized opportunities that drive long-run returns.
Gunther's axiom to always bet meaningfully warns that over-cautious stakes make even correct decisions irrelevant to wealth.
Stops do not guarantee the maximum loss in gaps and limit moves, and correlations jump in crises, so per-trade risk caps understate the real risk to capital.

operationalized_by.why: Sizing is based on risk of ruin from win rate, R:R and average loss rather than confidence, with an average loss of about 0.5% of allocated capital, and the page notes that a 50% drawdown needs a 100% gain.
Rule 8 caps risk by trade grade as a share of the daily stop (A+ up to 80%, A 30%, B 15%, C 5%).
Two losses end the day, and when volatility widens the structural stop to 40-50 NQ points the trader cuts contracts rather than moving the stop.
The daily limit is a maximum dollar or % loss rather than a trade count, illustrated by about $3,000 on a roughly $160,000 prop account.
Stop first, size second: the stop goes at real invalidation and size is reduced until the risk is acceptable, with caps of about 10% of float and 1% of volume.
It holds the recovery formula, the streak-loss formula 1 - (1-f)^k and the ruin approximation (q/p)^U used to check survivability.

measurable_as: Monte Carlo resample each setup's R-multiples at risk fractions of 0.25%, 0.5%, 1% and 2% and report the probability of reaching a 20%, 30% or 50% drawdown.
Compare terminal wealth and maximum drawdown at each fraction with an estimated Kelly fraction shrunk for estimation error.
Measure realised loss against planned loss per trade (slippage past stops, gaps) to quantify tail exposure.
Track portfolio heat (total open risk) and the average correlation of open positions against realised drawdowns.
Record drawdown depth and time to recover to check the loss asymmetry on the account's actual path.
gaps: Most playbooks do not state risk per trade or daily limits, so the KB cannot compare preservation practices across them.
No guidance on choosing a fraction of Kelly when the win rate is a wide-interval estimate from a discretionary journal.
No per-instrument data on gap risk or slippage beyond stops.
No note on the behavioural effects of drawdowns, that is, how a deep drawdown changes later decisions.

nodes.summary: A transaction fixes the terms of an exchange at one moment, not an objective or permanent value; participants disagree and revise their valuations. Fundamental, behavioural and statistical approaches each look for a usable relationship, and a gap between price and one's own value estimate starts an investigation rather than proving an edge, because the estimate may be wrong, the gap may persist, or costs may exceed the benefit.

grounded_in.why: AMT defines value as the area where two-sided trade is accepted over time and volume and lets it migrate, a market-generated idea of value distinct from any single transaction price.
The value area and POC are the measurable form of where participants have agreed to trade most.
Reversion to a reference fair value works in balanced regimes but carries negative skew when the regime turns, a price-value gap that can persist and hurt.
The fundamental approach estimates value from rates, growth and policy, and the note stresses that markets trade surprise versus consensus, not levels.
EMH holds that price already reflects available information, so an apparent discrepancy is usually compensation for risk or an error in the estimate.
Positioning and crowd beliefs show participants holding different valuations at the same price, as Section XV describes.
The forward-premium puzzle is a long-lived gap between a theoretical relationship and realised prices that the note explains as a crash-risk premium, a discrepancy that persists by design.

supported_by.why: Dalton's Market Profile treats value as what the auction accepts and separates day-timeframe traders from other-timeframe participants who move value.
Steidlmayer's original text frames the market as a self-organising auction of price, time and value.
Pedersen argues mispricings persist because of costs and limits to arbitrage, matching Section XV's warning that a gap may persist or cost more to exploit than it pays.
Harris catalogues participants who trade for reasons other than a view on value (hedgers, utilitarian traders), supporting that a trade price is not a shared valuation.
Ilmanen's synthesis of value, carry and momentum premia shows that price-value gaps often reflect compensated risk rather than free edge.
Marks's second-level thinking asks what is already reflected in price, the distinction between one's own value view and the market's.
Soros documents gaps between perception and reality opening and closing through boom-bust sequences.

challenged_by.why: If biased perceptions change the fundamentals they price, there is no independent value for price to return to, which complicates the value/price distinction and Section II's claim that the market exists independently of understanding.
Malkiel's case for efficiency implies most perceived discrepancies are illusions and that, after costs, investigating them rarely pays.
Livermore's maxim that the market is never wrong, only opinions are, treats price as the arbiter and warns that a private value estimate invites holding losing positions.

operationalized_by.why: Fair price is set by the event driving the market (the 9:30 ET open or the pre-news price) and dropped once value has clearly moved, and reversion is entered only after a DC or BOS confirmation.
Rule 2 locates fair value with the volume profile, setups 1-2 trade failed auctions back to fair value, and setup 3 accepts a breakout as new value only when price holds outside with participation.
Its scoring favours moves with no fundamental change (real news may have shifted equilibrium) and a quantifiable value anchor, and it targets only a partial retracement to the 20-period MA.
It runs two models chosen by market state: trend continuation toward new balance, and mean reversion to the prior POC after a failed breakout.
An Episodic Pivot requires months of neglect, a catalyst that changes the story and rapid repricing on a gap and volume, trading the market's re-rating of value.
Its post-earnings drift model enters after a positive reaction plus an EPS beat and holds about 60 trading days, built on the slow absorption of earnings news into price.

measurable_as: For each value reference (POC, VWAP, session open, 20-period MA), measure the probability and speed of return after a deviation of k ATR, conditioned on regime and on whether news was present.
Fit an Ornstein-Uhlenbeck half-life to deviations from fair value and check its stability across years.
Compare reversion rates for moves with and without a fundamental catalyst, following Breitstein's criterion.
Journal every perceived discrepancy that was investigated, traded or rejected, with its outcome net of costs.
gaps: The KB uses 'value' in at least three senses (auction value area, fundamental value, event-defined fair price) with no note reconciling them.
No concept note on fundamental valuation methods for single assets, such as cash-flow or relative valuation.
No empirical study in the KB of fair-value reversion rates by regime or after news.

nodes.summary: A compelling explanation is not a demonstrated advantage. Before acting, the trader examines the full distribution of outcomes, expected value after costs, and the uncertainty around every estimate.

grounded_in.why: E[R] = p*W - (1-p)*L is the core calculation the principle requires, and the note shows high win rates with negative expectancy.
The KB defines edge as positive expectancy after costs, a property of a distribution and never of a single trade.
Sharpe, profit factor, SQN, skew and kurtosis describe the distribution beyond its mean, including hidden tail risk.
Out-of-sample tests, walk-forward and the deflated Sharpe ratio guard against a backtest that justifies a trade only by chance.
Clean data, realistic costs, no look-ahead and Monte Carlo resampling are the procedures that produce the numbers the principle demands.
Skewed, fat-tailed outcome distributions are why the principle asks for the whole distribution and not just averages.
The breakeven win rate for a given R:R is the first mathematical check on any setup or marketing claim.

supported_by.why: Aronson applies data-snooping corrections and finds most technical rules fail rigorous tests, the reason explanations need mathematical support.
Taleb's point that a strategy can win often and still lose money (frequency versus magnitude) is the case for examining the distribution.
Wasserman covers inference, the bootstrap and multiple testing, the tools for putting uncertainty around an expected value.
Bailey and Lopez de Prado correct the Sharpe ratio for the number of trials and non-normal returns, measuring how much justification a backtest really provides.
Lopez de Prado's backtest-overfitting statistics and purged cross-validation set a standard for demonstrating an advantage on financial data.
Tharp's R-multiples, expectancy and SQN turn a trading idea into a measurable distribution.

challenged_by.why: Taleb shows the law of large numbers works slowly under fat tails, so an expectancy 'justified' from a few hundred trades can be false precision.
The note observes the setup appears only a few times a year, so any win rate rests on a tiny sample and rare high-conviction opportunities cannot be justified statistically before acting.
If edges appear and decay with the ecology of participants, an expectancy measured on past data may not apply now, however rigorous the calculation.

operationalized_by.why: E[R], the breakeven win rate, the standard error of a win rate, SQN and the deflated Sharpe ratio are the formulas the principle calls for.
Every trade is judged on EV = win rate x reward - loss probability x risk, and rule 8 scales size to setup quality.
Rules 5-8 backtest the exact rules, develop on 80% of history, freeze, test on the unseen 20%, and run shuffle and resampling Monte Carlo.

Rule 6's baseline filters (return-to-drawdown of at least 4, profit factor of at least 1.3-1.5, two or more trades a month) are followed by rule 7's parameter-robustness, out-of-sample, Monte Carlo and cross-market tests.
Rule 2 requires the expected move per trade to be large relative to costs, with the example of 0.2% round-trip costs taking half of a 0.4% edge.
Its risk section measures the prop evaluation pass rate under real rules rather than raw P&L and suggests about 50 evaluation backtests to reduce small-sample noise.

measurable_as: For each playbook, compute EV per trade in R after costs with a bootstrap confidence interval and the probability that EV > 0.
Check that the Wilson lower bound of the win rate exceeds the cost-adjusted breakeven win rate.
Compute the deflated Sharpe ratio given the number of variants tried.
Report skew, kurtosis and the share of total R that comes from the best 5% of trades.
Report the ratio of out-of-sample to in-sample expectancy.
gaps: No shared dataset of trade outcomes for the 47 playbooks; most cannot be checked because win rate or R:R is missing.
No standard cost assumptions per market.
The pre-trade checklist's 30-trade minimum is a heuristic that is not justified for fat-tailed, skewed R distributions.

nodes.summary: When the evidence is unclear or one's own framework cannot justify a trade, stay out of the market: waiting is better than entering for reasons the method does not support.

grounded_in.why: Precise written setup definitions and a regime on/off filter are what make 'the framework cannot justify it' checkable.
FOMO, revenge trading and overconfidence are the forces that push traders to force entries.
The KB treats running a setup outside its valid regime as the most common cause of failure, so a regime mismatch is a reason to stay out.
The checklist requires the defined confirmation to have completed, so an entry before it is a forced trade.
When higher and lower timeframes conflict the setup lacks agreement, a common no-trade condition in the playbooks.
Chasing worsens entry price and R:R, so a late entry can turn a valid setup into one the mathematics no longer supports.

supported_by.why: Livermore's losses from trading on tips and hope are the classic case of forcing trades without justification.
Tendler treats greed and FOMO as fixable flaws that produce trades outside the method.
Overconfidence and fast heuristic judgement explain why traders believe weak setups are good enough.
Taleb's noise-versus-signal argument supports waiting until the evidence is distinguishable from randomness.
The KB's synthesis finds the wizards share risk control and discipline across very different methods.

challenged_by.why: Rule 10 argues that waiting for confirmation gives up part of the edge, so a strict wait-until-clear rule has a cost in entry price.
Turtles who skipped signals they found unattractive failed, so if 'unclear' is judged in the moment, not forcing can turn into selectively skipping valid signals.

operationalized_by.why: A trade needs market state, location and aggression in that order, the trader stays flat if any one is missing, and rule 4 says no aggression means no trade.
Rule 9 lists no-trade conditions: timeframes disagree, balanced market, no liquidity taken, no order-flow confirmation, late entry, or risk that cannot be defined.
Rule 3 says no clear draw on liquidity means no trade, and rule 6 skips the setup and never chases if price does not retrace into the FVG.
Rule 2 says no liquidity built means no trade and to stand aside, and a setup that does not form inside the session window is not taken.
Rule 6 skips any setup that cannot take a clean 10-point stop, and rule 9 filters out partial setups away from a level.
Rule 8's no-trade list includes an extended breakout the trader would be chasing and any base too messy to define invalidation.

measurable_as: Tag trades taken with one or more plan conditions missing and compare their expectancy with fully qualified trades.
Measure entry distance from the planned level in R and its relation to outcome.
Count trades outside the defined session window and their R.
Shadow-log no-trade days and estimate the expected value given up by waiting.
gaps: No objective, testable definition of 'the evidence is unclear' in the KB.
No data compares anticipation and confirmation entries on the same setups, although the KB names this as a genuine conflict.
No record of skipped setups to estimate the cost of not forcing.

nodes.summary: When evidence changes, first manage the existing risk, then investigate the change and revise the hypothesis if warranted, avoiding both impulsive reaction and the defence of a disproven idea.

grounded_in.why: Structural and time stops placed where the idea is wrong are the predefined way to manage risk first.
The distinction between continuation (BOS) and change of character (CHoCH) tells whether changed price action actually refutes the hypothesis.
Investigating a change often means checking whether the regime has shifted, which can flip a setup's expectancy.
The review loop is where the investigation is recorded and the hypothesis formally revised.
Bayesian updating is the methodical alternative to both impulsive reversal and stubborn defence.
Invalidation written before entry makes the first response mechanical rather than emotional.

supported_by.why: Popper holds hypotheses provisionally and abandons them when refuted, the stance behind not defending a disproven hypothesis.
Soros acts on a hypothesis while looking for its flaw and records his changes of mind in a diary, a model of methodical revision.
Predefining and fully accepting risk removes the hesitation that turns changed evidence into an impulsive or frozen response.
Taking small losses instantly is the 'manage existing risk' step done without drama.
Dalio's practice of systematising lessons from mistakes is the investigate-and-revise half of the principle.
Probability as extended logic gives the rule for updating belief in a hypothesis as evidence arrives.

challenged_by.why: Price often runs the stops beyond an obvious invalidation level and then reverses, so an immediate risk response can exit just before the hypothesis is vindicated.
Its approach replaces a tight stop with a position small enough to lose entirely, deliberately holding through adverse moves rather than reacting to them.
Its strict, early breakeven rule reacts quickly to adverse movement and the page admits it produces a high breakeven rate, showing that fast defensive responses also cost expectancy.

operationalized_by.why: After three failed reversion trades in a session, reversions stop for that session, and rule 9 drops an old fair price once value has clearly moved.
Rule 9 accepts a failed level: when price breaks a wall with strength and holds, the trader stops fading it and reassesses.
Rule 12 benches a strategy only when drawdown nears its Monte Carlo maximum or underperformance persists, never on short-term losses alone.
Rule 11 treats a breach of the Monte Carlo range as a trigger for review, not proof that the strategy is broken.
Rule 9 holds while the controlling side stays in control and exits when the opposite side takes over, tying the exit to the evidence for the trade.
Its invalidation is a reclaim of the previous day's close that holds, with an immediate exit and no holding in hope.

measurable_as: Measure the delay between an invalidation trigger and the actual exit, and its cost in R.
Track what share of hypothesis revisions were preceded by a journaled investigation.
Record the price path after invalidation exits to estimate how often exits fall on detours.
Compare later expectancy of revised setups with unrevised ones.
gaps: No KB procedure says what evidence, and how much, is required before revising a hypothesis.
No data on how often stops are run at structural invalidation levels.

nodes.summary: A loss does not by itself mean a bad decision and a win does not by itself mean a good one; the trader evaluates the process and the result together.

grounded_in.why: The note's consequence that a single trade's outcome is not feedback on the decision, with Duke's warning against 'resulting', is the principle itself.
Edge belongs to the distribution of outcomes, so decision quality is judged by expected value, not by one result.
Rule-adherence and setup-grade fields record process quality separately from the R result.
SQN and confidence-adjusted metrics judge results over a sample, where outcome evidence becomes meaningful.
Normal losing streaks show that runs of bad outcomes are compatible with sound decisions.
A written plan is the benchmark that defines whether a decision followed or broke the process.

supported_by.why: Duke's book is built on separating decision quality from outcome.
Duke is the KB's main voice for process over outcome and the 'resulting' error.
Douglas's random distribution of wins and losses for any edge means individual results say little about the decision.
Douglas's five fundamental truths underpin the KB's probabilistic-thinking note.
Taleb's alternative histories judge a decision by the outcomes it could have produced.
Poker analytics evaluates decisions under uncertainty by expected value, a setting where sound plays lose individual hands.

challenged_by.why: Livermore's view that the market is never wrong and opinions are makes the outcome the final arbiter, a warning that 'good process' can become an excuse for poor reasoning.
Under fat tails, years of outcomes may be needed to separate skill from luck, so for a long time process evaluation rests largely on the trader's own judgment.
Seykota's claim that everybody gets what they want from the market treats outcome patterns as evidence about the trader's process and intentions.

operationalized_by.why: Rule 17 journals mistakes, emotional state and a trade grade, and grades the process, not the P&L.
Stage 4 judges consistency by execution rather than outcome, week over week.
Rule 12 counts a runner stopped at breakeven as a successful trade, defining success by execution.
The daily report card logs process mistakes without judgment, separately from results.
Its review tracks performance by setup grade, so quality and outcome are compared over a sample.
The standard error of an estimated win rate (about +/-7% at n = 50) shows how little a short run of outcomes proves.

measurable_as: Fill a 2x2 table of process followed or not x win or loss and compare expectancy and frequency by cell.
Score each trade's process before seeing the result and test whether process scores predict R over rolling samples.
Compute how many trades are needed before the confidence interval on expectancy excludes zero.
gaps: No KB rubric for scoring decision quality; the playbooks that grade trades leave their criteria unspecified.
No guidance on blinding the process score from the outcome to avoid hindsight bias.

nodes.summary: The market is a system of relationships whose visible expression is price. The trader builds a fallible model of it, treats every expected path as a hypothesis, estimates conditional probabilities from defined conditions and adequate samples, uses mathematics (expected value after costs, full distributions, out-of-sample evidence) to test beliefs, acts only when understanding, evidence and mathematics agree, protects capital and process, and records everything so that the philosophy itself can be tested.

grounded_in.why: Section I's claim that price is the visible result of participants' interactions is the KB's definition of microstructure: how orders become prices.
Conditional probability (Sections V-VI) and A->C->B (Section III) both depend on defining the conditions or regime in which a pattern appears.
The philosophy aims at a repeatable, positive-expectancy advantage after costs, the KB's definition of edge.
Section VII's expected-value formula is the KB's expectancy concept with a cost term.
Treating the future as uncertain and separating decisions from outcomes runs through Sections VI, XI and XXI.
Section XVII's separation of hypothesis development from evaluation, and its demand for out-of-sample tests, is this concept.
Section XIV's loss asymmetry and survival argument rest on drawdown and ruin mathematics.
Section XVI makes the journal the record through which understanding is tested.

supported_by.why: Named in Section XX as a microstructure starting point for how market structure shapes observed prices.
Named in Section XX; its econometrics of trades and quotes studies price as the result of order interaction.
Kahneman's prospect theory, which Section XX names, underpins the behavioural sections.
Aronson's scientific-method approach to trading rules matches Section XVII's programme.
Duke's separation of decision quality from outcome is Section XI and Principle 8.
Soros's fallibilism and his diary of hypotheses mirror the system-versus-model distinction and the journal.
Lo's adaptive markets view, in which tendencies recur but edges appear and decay, matches 'recurrence is not repetition'.
Vince's sizing geometry, where leverage drives both growth and ruin, supports Section XIV.

challenged_by.why: Soros's thesis that participants' views change the fundamentals they price challenges Section II's claim that the market exists independently of the trader's understanding.
Weak-form efficiency implies past price patterns carry little exploitable information, a direct challenge to the recurring-storyline premise.
Taleb shows the law of large numbers converges slowly under fat tails, weakening the sample-based probability estimates Section VI relies on.

operationalized_by.why: Its L0-L8 pipeline from 'is there an edge?' to 'is it still working?' is the KB's operating version of the philosophy's sequence.
Its ten gates turn understanding, evidence, mathematics, sizing and state of mind into a scored pre-trade check.
It collects the expectancy, sizing, ruin and validation formulas the philosophy calls for.
The nine-layer stack (edge, mechanics, context, lens, setup, execution, risk, psychology, review) gives each section of the philosophy a layer.
Its rules that win-rate claims need a sample size and an R:R, and that backtests are hypotheses until tested out of sample, apply Sections VI, VII and XVII to evidence quality.
Its idea, cause, rules, backtest, out-of-sample, Monte Carlo and monitoring sequence is the playbook closest to Section XVII's scientific method.

measurable_as: Track adherence to each of the 12 principles per trade in the journal and relate adherence scores to risk-adjusted results over rolling samples.
Restate each section as a falsifiable hypothesis and record its test status and evidence.
Compare the trade set that passed every gate with the rest on expectancy, drawdown and out-of-sample stability.
gaps: No empirical test of the philosophy as a whole exists; Section XIX itself says internal coherence is not proof of profitability.
Madhavan's microstructure survey and Kahneman and Tversky's prospect-theory paper, both named in Section XX, have no node in the allowed index.

extension_candidates.title: Name the counterparty: understanding as a causal account of who is on the other side
extension_candidates.idea: The edge note says an edge needs a structural reason someone is on the other side (forced liquidation, hedging flow, stop clusters, behavioural bias, a risk premium or an information lag), and the unified framework opens L0 by asking who that counterparty is and why. Section VIII asks for a defensible explanation without saying what makes it defensible. Naming the counterparty and its motive would make the understanding leg checkable. Matteo Conti adds that knowing the cause also tells you when the edge has stopped applying.

extension_candidates.title: Monte Carlo bands as the 'expected range of outcomes'
extension_candidates.idea: Sections X and XI ask whether results fall within the strategy's expected variation but give no procedure for checking. Two playbooks supply one. Shuffle or resample the trade list to get distributions of drawdowns and losing streaks, then monitor live results against those bands. A breach triggers a review, not proof of failure. A failing strategy is benched (size cut or moved back to simulation), not deleted. Lo's point that edges decay as markets adapt is the reason the bands need re-estimating.

extension_candidates.title: Graded conviction instead of a binary trade/no-trade
extension_candidates.idea: The philosophy treats an opportunity as either present or absent. Several sources instead size by the strength of the evidence. Jeff Holden allocates a share of the daily stop by grade: up to 80% for A+, 5% for C. Candace Lau and Lance Breitstein size by the number and quality of confluences. Meta-labeling sizes a discretionary signal by a model's estimated probability of success, and Kelly is the theory that bet size should scale with edge. Together these would make Principles 5, 6 and 9 continuous rules rather than yes/no ones.

extension_candidates.title: Emotional state as a risk budget with its own stop rules
extension_candidates.idea: Section XII treats emotion as interference to resist. The knowledge base treats state as a measurable input with its own stop rules. Tendler weighs the emotional expected value of the next trade, collects data on warning signs, and ends the session if the reset limit is broken. Umar Ashraf reads being overwhelmed by emotion as a sign the size is too big. Fixed behavioural stops apply, such as two losses ending the day. Coates finds that hormonal cycles shift risk appetite. All of this suggests protecting the process partly through structure (size, session limits) rather than willpower alone.

extension_candidates.title: Stepping back has a cost and must be defined in advance
extension_candidates.idea: Faith reports that failed Turtles skipped signals and so missed the large winners in the distribution. The probabilistic-thinking note says skipping valid setups destroys the sample the edge depends on. Pavel argues that waiting for confirmation gives up part of the edge, and consensus-and-conflicts lists anticipation versus confirmation as an unresolved trade-off. Section IX and Principle 6 would be stronger with two additions: write 'unclear' as a testable condition before the session, and log skipped setups so the cost of waiting can be measured.

extension_candidates.title: Growth versus survival: choosing the risk fraction
extension_candidates.idea: Section XIV argues from the asymmetry of losses but never says how much to risk. The knowledge base adds the growth side of the trade-off. Kelly sizing maximises long-run growth. Betting more than twice Kelly gives negative growth even with an edge, and full Kelly brings deep drawdowns. Because win rates are estimates with error, fractional Kelly is the safer choice. In prop accounts the trailing drawdown, not the account size, is the effective bankroll. Together these give a way to choose a risk fraction, not just to cap it.

extension_candidates.title: Value as what the auction accepts, and why gaps persist
extension_candidates.idea: Section XV contrasts price with an estimate of value but never defines value in operational terms. Auction market theory does: value is where trade is accepted over time and volume, it can migrate, and acceptance versus rejection separates a new value from a failed excursion. JJ Simon resets fair price to whatever event is now driving the market and drops it once value has moved. Breitstein discounts reversion when real news may have shifted equilibrium. Pedersen's limits to arbitrage explain why a known gap can persist.

extension_candidates.title: Invalidation levels are liquidity
extension_candidates.idea: Section X says to act first on predefined invalidation. The liquidity notes show that stops cluster beyond obvious swing levels and are often run before price reverses, which is an A to C to B detour produced by order flow. Sweep-reversal playbooks wait for displacement or a structure shift after the sweep, and put stops beyond the sweep extreme. The philosophy could address where invalidation sits relative to resting stops, not only whether it is set in advance.

nodes.summary: The market is a web of participants whose transactions leave price as their visible trace; because the future cannot be known, the trader acts only when a defensible explanation, present evidence and a cost-adjusted expected-value assessment agree, sizes so that being wrong is survivable, and keeps testing beliefs through a journal and a scientific method.

grounded_in.why: Sections I, IV and XX.1 treat price as the outcome of orders meeting liquidity between participants with different beliefs, which is the subject of microstructure.
Sections V, VI and VIII make every pattern and probability conditional on the current market state, which the KB models as regimes (trend/range, high/low volatility).
Sections VI and XI put probability, not prediction, at the base of decisions and separate decision quality from a single outcome, the core of the thinking-in-bets note.
Section VII's expected value net of trading costs is the KB's expectancy formula and the philosophy's main quantitative test.
Section VIII's opportunity and the manifesto's 'seek an edge, test it' match the KB definition of edge as a repeatable condition with positive expectancy after costs.
Sections XVII and XX.4 require separating development from evaluation and testing out of sample, the defences listed in the overfitting note.
Section XIV's 50%-loss-needs-100% example is the recovery-asymmetry formula of the risk-of-ruin note, and survival is a precondition of the whole method.
Sections XII and XIII locate the main threat to the process in fear, greed, frustration and the pull of money, the territory of the psychology note.
Section XVI and Principle 11 make the journal the feedback loop by which beliefs are compared with market behaviour, which is the KB's L8 review concept.

supported_by.why: Harris, named in Section XX.1, explains who trades and why and how market structure and dealers shape observed prices and costs.
Hasbrouck, named in Section XX.1, gives the econometrics of how trades and quotes reveal information, the formal side of 'price as expression of a relationship'.
Douglas argues that consistency comes from a probabilistic mindset, objectively defined edges and risk accepted before entry, the same stance as Sections VI, XI and XII.
Duke's argument that decision quality must be separated from outcome is the independent statement of Section XI and Principle 8.
Kahneman, named in Section XX.3, documents the biases (loss aversion, overconfidence, hindsight) that the philosophy's process is built to guard against.
Aronson applies the scientific method and data-snooping corrections to technical rules, the programme Section XVII sets out.
Lo's view that edges are conditional on an evolving market ecology supports Sections V and VI's insistence that probabilities hold only under defined conditions.
Tharp makes expectancy in R-multiples and position sizing the drivers of results, matching Sections VII and XIV.

challenged_by.why: Soros's reflexivity holds that participants' biased views change the fundamentals they price, which cuts against Section II's claim that the market exists independently of the trader's understanding of it.

If weak-form efficiency holds at the trader's horizon, the recurring storylines of Section V are mostly noise, so the philosophy's premise that conditional tendencies can be found and exploited is itself a hypothesis to test.
Taleb shows that under fat tails sample means converge slowly and the law of large numbers works far more slowly than the philosophy's reliance on repeated observations (Section VI) assumes.

operationalized_by.why: The L0 to L8 pipeline (edge, mechanics, context, lens, setup, trigger, size, discipline, review) is the KB's step-by-step version of the philosophy's sequence from understanding to review.
Its ten scored gates (edge with logged instances, regime, invalidation, size, state of mind) turn Principles 1 to 10 into a go/no-go test before each trade.
It holds the formulas the philosophy depends on: expectancy, the standard error of a win rate, recovery after drawdown, streak damage and the deflated Sharpe ratio.
The 9-layer stack is the routing scheme that lets each section of the philosophy be mapped to a layer (L0 maths through L8 validation).

Its 13-step process (explain why the edge should exist, fix objective rules, develop on 80% in sample, freeze, test on the unseen 20%, Monte Carlo, monitor live against simulated ranges) is the philosophy's scientific method carried out end to end.
Its foundational rule that the goal is a repeatable process with money as a by-product, plus mandatory journaling at every stage, expresses Sections XII, XIII and XVI.

measurable_as: For each setup in the journal: out-of-sample expectancy in R after measured costs, with a confidence interval, compared with the in-sample estimate.
Calibration of recorded pre-trade probability estimates against realised hit rates, bucketed by stated probability and by market condition.
R distribution of trades that passed all three elements of Section VIII versus trades taken when they disagreed.
Monte Carlo probability of a 20% and a 50% drawdown at the chosen risk fraction, using the journal's own R-multiples.
Rule-adherence rate over time and its relation to outcome, to test whether following the process improves decisions.
gaps: No audited or independently replicated track record exists in the KB for any strategy, so the philosophy's claim that the method can produce an edge is untested.
The KB has no study linking adherence to the philosophy's principles with trading outcomes.
The research papers Section XX points to (Madhavan's survey, Kahneman and Tversky's 1979 paper) have no linkable node in the allowed id index; only Kahneman's book and person node are available.
Reflexivity and market efficiency, the two strongest objections to Sections II and V, are not reconciled with the philosophy anywhere in the KB.

nodes.summary: The journal should record the growth and testing of understanding, not just fills and P&L: conditions, reasoning, probability estimate and invalidation written before or at decision time, then a review of whether the outcome fell in the expected range, the plan was followed and emotion intervened, so that beliefs can be compared with market behaviour without hindsight reconstruction.

grounded_in.why: The note lists the fields (setup tag and grade, regime label, rule adherence, emotion tags, R, MAE/MFE) and the daily, weekly and monthly review cadence that Section XVI describes.
Section XVI's 'what would invalidate the hypothesis' and 'was the trade executed according to plan' presuppose rules written before the trade, the subject of the trading-plan note.
The question of whether a result 'was simply one outcome within an uncertain process' is the KB's point that one trade's outcome is not feedback on the decision.
The journal's purpose of testing whether a setup deserves a 'high probability' label requires expectancy per setup, which the journal note names as the reason for setup tags.
Section XVI's example of a strategy that works under some conditions and fails under others needs a regime label on every trade, a field the journal note includes.
Per-setup statistics (profit factor, expectancy, SQN) are the measures a journal produces when beliefs are compared with results.
The backtesting note's warning about hindsight bias and lenient rule reading, and its fix of writing rules first and logging every instance, is the same discipline Section XVI asks of a journal.
Section XVI's question 'did emotions influence the decision?' depends on the emotion tags and adherence flags the psychology and journal notes recommend.

supported_by.why: Soros's 1985 to 1986 real-time diary records his hypotheses, positions and changes of mind, a published example of a journal of understanding rather than of P&L.
Duke's case against judging a decision by its result supports reviewing the reasoning behind a decision separately from how it turned out.
Kahneman's account of hindsight and outcome bias explains why Section XVI insists that reasoning be recorded before or at the decision, not reconstructed later.
Brandt runs classical charting as a business with trade logs and risk rules, a practitioner model of the written record Section XVI describes.
Steenbarger applies structured self-observation to change trading patterns, which is the journal used as a tool for learning.
Steenbarger's self-coaching lessons rest on reviewing one's own records, supporting the journal as the basis for improvement.
Dalio's practice of systematising lessons from mistakes supports turning experience into a record that can be examined instead of relying on memory.

challenged_by.why: Slicing a journal by setup, regime, session and emotion creates many comparisons, so some slice will look strong or weak by chance; the 'differences' Section XVI hopes to discover can be multiple-testing artefacts unless the slices are fixed in advance.
Taleb argues that looking at results too often mostly shows noise, which complicates a post-trade review of every outcome and risks reading meaning into random variation.

operationalized_by.why: Rule 17 journals every trade while fresh (entry, exit, stop, target, size, partials, setup type, planned or not, mistakes, emotional state, grade) and grades the process rather than the P&L.
Rules 1 to 5 log every meaningful mistake in a daily report card for a week, pick one, find its root cause with five whys and turn it into a specific, measurable playbook fix.
Rule 10 makes a post-session journal a cool-down that records what was felt, when focus slipped and an If-Then plan, and rule 3 collects warning-sign data for weeks.
Rule 8 makes journaling mandatory at every stage, and Stage 2 collects win rate, per-setup and time-of-day statistics from the journal.
Its post-trade step logs setup tag, grade, regime, session, MAE/MFE, adherence and emotion, the fields needed to test beliefs against results.

measurable_as: Calibration: bucket the probability estimates recorded before entry and compare each bucket with its realised hit rate (Brier score, reliability diagram).
Hindsight control: share of trades whose pre-trade fields carry a timestamp before the entry time and were never edited afterwards.
Contradiction check: realised win rate and expectancy of trades labelled 'high probability' versus all trades, with confidence intervals.
Condition dependence: expectancy per setup by pre-defined regime label, tested for a difference with a pre-specified interaction test rather than post-hoc slicing.
Invalidation discipline: fraction of losing trades closed because the recorded invalidation occurred versus for other reasons.
gaps: The KB's journal concept note has no field for a pre-trade probability estimate or a timestamp rule against hindsight; the fuller template lives in 00_philosophy/journal-template.md, which has no node id.
Nothing in the KB covers forecast calibration scoring (Brier score, reliability diagrams), the natural test of recorded probability estimates.
No guidance on the minimum number of journal entries per condition before a 'performs well under X' conclusion is drawn, beyond the checklist's 30-instance rule of thumb.
No study in the KB shows that journaling improves trading results; support is practitioner (T2) and psychology literature.

nodes.summary: A philosophy becomes a trading method only when its claims are written as precise rules that can be found consistently in historical data, tested net of costs on data not used to build them, and examined across market conditions, with hypothesis development kept separate from evaluation so the rules do not learn the noise of the past.

grounded_in.why: Section XVII's steps (define the behaviour, check whether the move occurred, measure gains and losses with costs) are the systematic-backtesting checklist: clean data, realistic costs, no look-ahead, out-of-sample tests.
The warning about adjusting rules until they fit the past is the KB's overfitting problem, with holdout, walk-forward, parameter robustness and deflated Sharpe as defences.
Whether the strategy 'would have remained profitable under realistic conditions' is a test of expectancy after costs.
Section XVII asks whether performance differs across market conditions and whether deterioration means the market changed, which is regime analysis.
Measuring gains, losses and their variation calls on the KB's metrics (Sharpe, profit factor, max drawdown, SQN, skew).
The method's goal is to decide whether a believed advantage is a repeatable positive-expectancy condition, the KB's definition of edge.
The note's points that almost every pattern is an autocorrelation claim and that structural breaks require rolling or walk-forward estimates are the statistical basis of Section XVII's tests.
Purged and embargoed cross-validation and leakage control are the KB's tools for keeping development and evaluation separate when labels overlap in time.

supported_by.why: Aronson argues for the scientific method and data-snooping-robust tests in technical analysis and finds most rules fail them, the same discipline Section XVII asks for.
López de Prado sets out purged cross-validation and backtest-overfitting statistics that make the separation of development and evaluation precise.
The deflated Sharpe ratio corrects a backtest's Sharpe for the number of trials, skew and kurtosis, a formal answer to 'adjusting rules until they fit the past'.
Davey describes a champion trader's process for developing, validating and monitoring systems, a practitioner version of Section XVII.
Carver's framework for systematic rules stresses avoiding overfitting and keeping rules simple, matching 'the simplest framework that adequately measures'.
Popper's falsifiability criterion is the philosophical root of 'a theory becomes a trading method only when its claims can be tested against actual outcomes'.
Wasserman covers inference, the bootstrap, hypothesis testing and multiple testing, the statistical tools the method needs.
The talk attributes most quant-fund failures to process errors such as backtest overfitting, independent support for separating research from evaluation.

challenged_by.why: If market efficiency evolves with its participants, a rule validated out of sample is tested on a population that is already changing, so passing the test cannot license confidence in the next period the way a repeatable laboratory experiment would.
A few years of out-of-sample data may contain no tail event, so a negatively skewed strategy can pass Section XVII's tests and still carry hidden blow-up risk.

It records discretionary versus systematic trading as a genuine conflict; many practitioner lenses rely on judgment that resists being defined 'clearly enough to identify it consistently in historical data'.

operationalized_by.why: Rules 3 and 6 to 8 define entry, exit and size with no room for interpretation, tune only on an 80% in-sample split, freeze the rules before testing the unseen 20%, then run Monte Carlo shuffle and resampling.

Rule 7 tries to break each strategy with parameter-robustness, in-sample/out-of-sample periods spanning different regimes, Monte Carlo drawdown and cross-market tests, and rule 2 caps entries at two or three rules to limit curve fitting.
Rule 2 checks expected move per trade against fees, spread and slippage, and rules 4 to 7 tell the trader to research the exact thresholds and time exits for each market.
The playbook backtests the account model by its evaluation pass rate under the firm's real rules and suggests about 50 runs to reduce small-sample noise.
Its L8 block gives the expected best Sharpe from N skill-less trials, the deflated Sharpe ratio and profit factor, the arithmetic of Section XVII's tests.
Its L8 stage compares live with backtest, deflates Sharpe for the number of trials and uses walk-forward testing.

measurable_as: Out-of-sample to in-sample ratio of expectancy and Sharpe for rules frozen before the holdout was viewed.
Deflated Sharpe ratio or probability of backtest overfitting computed with the actual number of variants tried.
Parameter-sensitivity surface: whether performance forms a plateau or a spike across neighbouring parameter values.
Break-even cost per side and net expectancy under 1x, 2x and 3x the assumed costs.
Performance by regime bucket using cut-offs fixed on in-sample data only.
Whether live drawdowns and losing streaks stay within the Monte Carlo percentile bands of the backtest.
gaps: No KB note explains how to log the number of research trials so that deflated Sharpe or PBO can be computed; the evidence lab does this but has no node id.
Most Chart Fanatics playbooks leave key terms undefined (for example 'displacement', 'balanced', 'expanded' volatility), so their rules cannot yet be coded and tested.
Cost and slippage assumptions are missing even from the two systematic frameworks (Matteo Conti and Naoufel Taief list them as unspecified).
The concept notes give the standard error of a win rate but no statistical-power guidance on how many trades a test needs.

nodes.summary: The philosophy is condensed into twelve working principles: understand before acting, read movements in context, treat the future as uncertain, use probability conditionally, demand mathematical justification, do not force trades, respond to new evidence methodically, separate decision quality from outcomes, protect capital and emotional independence, record and investigate, and put the process before money.

grounded_in.why: A doctrine of principles is put into force as rules written before the trade, the trading-plan concept.
Principle 2's reading of a short-term move within its broader context is the KB's top-down, multi-timeframe analysis.
Principles 2 and 4 make the meaning of a pattern depend on market conditions, the regime concept.
Principle 5 asks for the distribution of outcomes, expected value and costs, the expectancy note's content.
Principles 3 and 8 (destination as hypothesis, losses not proof of bad decisions) restate the probabilistic-thinking note.
Principle 9 is a sizing rule: size so unfavourable sequences cannot end the trader's ability to continue.
Principles 6, 10 and 12 guard against forcing trades, emotional override and the pull of money, the psychology note's guardrails.
Principle 11 names the journal as the instrument by which accumulated evidence improves decisions.

supported_by.why: Douglas's seven principles of consistency (identify edges objectively, predefine and accept risk, act without hesitation, monitor errors) are an independent doctrine with the same core.
Schwager's interviews find that top traders use very different methods but share risk control and discipline, supporting a doctrine of principles rather than a single setup.
Elder's three Ms (mind, method, money) and fixed per-trade and monthly risk caps parallel the doctrine's split into understanding, mathematics, capital and psychology.
Schwager's 40 lessons from hedge-fund managers on process, risk and adaptation independently support principles 7, 9 and 11.
Duke's separation of decision quality from outcome independently argues Principle 8.
The Turtle experiment showed that a simple, written rule set can be taught, and that most failures came from not following it, supporting doctrine plus disciplined execution.

challenged_by.why: Gunther's rival twelve axioms (bet meaningfully, take profits early) conflict with Principle 9's survival-first sizing and with Principle 5's expectancy logic, which shows that compact doctrines can disagree and must be tested rather than adopted.
Druckenmiller argues for concentration over diversification and recounts Soros doubling the 1992 sterling short, a successful practice that pulls against uniformly small, survival-first sizing.
Tharp's claim that entries are overrated and that exits and sizing drive results (his random-entry experiments) questions Principle 1's priority on understanding before acting.

operationalized_by.why: Its ten scored lines (edge, regime, HTF bias, invalidation, size, state of mind, with fewer than 7 of 10 meaning no trade) put most of the twelve principles into one gate.
Its L0 to L8 stages map one-to-one onto the doctrine: edge and maths (P4, P5), context (P2), sizing (P9), discipline (P10) and review (P11).
Its rule that a trade needs market state, location and aggression in order, and that the trader stays flat if any is missing, plus 0.25 to 0.5% risk per trade, enacts Principles 2, 6 and 9.
Rule 8, the Three-Loss Rule (three failed reversions in one session stop reversions for that session), is a concrete instance of Principle 7's methodical response to changed evidence.
Rule 1's foundational principles (the goal is a repeatable process, control what you can, no single green month proves anything) and rule 8's mandatory journaling express Principles 8, 11 and 12.

measurable_as: Twelve adherence flags per trade in the journal, and the R distribution of fully adherent trades versus trades with any violation.
Dose-response: relation between the number of principles violated on a trade and its R outcome.
Logged no-trade decisions when the three elements disagreed, and the forward outcome of the skipped setups.
Frequency of each violation type over time, to find which principles are hardest to keep.
gaps: The KB does not translate the principles into numeric thresholds (what risk fraction satisfies Principle 9, what sample satisfies Principle 5).
Principles 2 and 7 need an operational test of 'the structure has changed'; the playbooks that come closest leave it unspecified (for example Fabio Valentini's balance test).
There is no evidence beyond practitioner testimony that following such a rule set improves results.

nodes.summary: Internal coherence is not profitability: the philosophy still has to show that some behaviours are repeatable, that conditions can be measured consistently, that probability estimates are reliable, that edges survive costs and changing conditions, and that the trader can execute consistently, and it must say what evidence would prove it wrong.

grounded_in.why: All six questions ask whether a believed advantage is a real, repeatable positive-expectancy condition after costs.
The worry that 'some patterns appear by chance' is the multiple-testing problem at the centre of the overfitting note.
Questions 2 and 5 are about defining market conditions and about whether a relationship survives when they change.
Question 4 asks whether expectancy stays positive after spreads, commissions, slippage and financing.
The costs listed in Question 4 (slippage, execution conditions) are the subject of the market-impact and execution-cost note.
Whether any behaviour is genuinely repeatable is the efficient-markets debate, resolved in the KB through the adaptive-markets view.
Question 6, whether the trader can execute consistently, depends on the discipline and emotional factors in the psychology note.
The answers have to come from research and testing, the backtesting note's domain.

supported_by.why: Popper's falsifiability underlies Section XIX's demand that a serious philosophy state what evidence would show it is wrong.
Aronson's finding that most technical rules fail rigorous testing supports treating repeatability as an open question rather than a premise.
Taleb shows how survivorship and luck masquerade as skill, independent support for 'some patterns appear by chance'.
Lo's argument that edges appear and decay as participants adapt supports Question 5 on changing market conditions.
Pedersen ties the existence of hedge-fund strategies to costs and limits to arbitrage, supporting Question 4's focus on whether an edge survives costs.
Bailey and López de Prado quantify how many trials inflate apparent performance, supporting Question 3's doubt about historical success rates.
Soros's use of his own fallibility as a method (form a hypothesis, act on it, look for what is wrong) is the same posture as keeping the philosophy open to investigation.

challenged_by.why: Under fat tails some of these questions cannot be answered to useful precision within one trader's sample, so 'establishing what evidence would demonstrate it is wrong' may need more data than is available.

Schwager's traders with exceptional audited records show edges in many idiosyncratic forms, often developed through live practice, which suggests some real edges may not reduce to the measurable, repeatable behaviours Questions 1 and 2 look for.

operationalized_by.why: Rule 2 requires an explanation of why each edge should exist (so the trader notices when it stops applying), and rule 11 monitors live results against Monte Carlo ranges.
Its approach of generating many strategies and trading only those that survive deliberate attempts to break them (rule 7) treats every strategy as a hypothesis that must earn its place.
Its rules of evidence (win-rate claims need a sample size and an R:R; backtests are hypotheses until checked out of sample) set the evidential bar the six questions require.
It provides the standard error of a win rate, the per-trade cost formula and the deflated Sharpe ratio, the tools for Questions 3, 4 and 1.
Its table of claims that do not survive scrutiny (for example a 90% win rate at 1:20 R:R) shows the KB already applying Section XIX's scepticism to practitioner claims.

measurable_as: Q1: out-of-sample persistence of a conditional frequency against a null adjusted for multiple testing.
Q2: agreement between two independent labellings of the same market condition.
Q3: width of confidence intervals and calibration of probability estimates out of sample.
Q4: net expectancy and break-even cost after measured spreads and slippage.
Q5: performance across regime buckets and sub-periods, with structural-break tests.
Q6: live versus backtest gap split into missed signals, slippage and rule violations.
For each hypothesis, a pre-registered falsification criterion and whether it was met.
gaps: No strategy note in the KB states explicit falsification criteria.
There is no live-trading dataset in the KB; the evidence lab's own summary says Questions 1, 2, 5 and 6 remain mostly open, with only a handful of markets and two periods tested.
No measured transaction-cost data exists for any instrument or session.

nodes.summary: Five research fields support and test the philosophy: market microstructure (how interaction produces price), probability and statistical inference (what history can establish), behavioural finance (as a source of hypotheses, not stories), backtest-overfitting research (why random patterns look convincing) and risk management (how sizing and drawdowns govern survival).

grounded_in.why: Section XX.1 names microstructure (order flow, liquidity, information, participant behaviour) as the field behind 'price as the interaction of participants'.
Liquidity is one of the mechanisms Section XX.1 lists as shaping the prices traders observe.
Section XX.2 lists probability distributions, variance and statistical dependence, the content of the distributions and fat-tails note.
Section XX.3's behavioural finance (overconfidence, loss aversion, the disposition effect) is the behavioural root of the psychology note.
Section XX.4's backtest-overfitting research is the subject of the overfitting and edge-validation note.
Section XX.4 warns that a strategy can look profitable in historical data without a real advantage, the central caution of the backtesting note.
Section XX.5 ties risk management to drawdowns and the ability to survive unfavourable outcomes, the risk-of-ruin note's subject.
Section XX.5 names position sizing and leverage as the levers of survival.

supported_by.why: Named in Section XX.1, it is the empirical text on how trades and quotes reveal information and form prices.
Named in Section XX.1, Harris explains who trades and why, liquidity and the components of transaction costs.
O'Hara's inventory and information models (Kyle, Glosten-Milgrom) are the theoretical core of the microstructure field Section XX.1 points to.
Kahneman, whose prospect theory with Tversky Section XX.3 names, covers loss aversion and the heuristics behind traders abandoning their methods.
A standard text on estimation and hypothesis testing, the statistical inference Section XX.2 calls for.
A central paper of the backtest-overfitting research Section XX.4 describes, correcting performance for the number of trials.
Vince shows how leverage drives both growth and ruin, the risk-management lesson of Section XX.5.
McNeil, Frey and Embrechts treat extreme-value theory and risk measures, the rigorous form of 'the distribution of returns affects survival'.

challenged_by.why: Taleb argues that standard inference tools (variance, confidence intervals, the law of large numbers) can mislead under fat tails, so the Section XX.2 toolkit needs fat-tail-aware methods.
Section XX omits the efficient-markets literature, whose weak-form claim is the null every recurring pattern must beat; leaving it out risks testing against the wrong benchmark.

Section XX.3 treats behavioural findings as sources of hypotheses about traders' errors, while reflexivity holds that participants' biases also change prices and fundamentals, a feedback channel the research list does not include.

operationalized_by.why: Partition 06's tracks (probability and statistics, time series, microstructure and execution, risk and sizing, quant validation) are organised reading paths for four of Section XX's five fields.

It traces the roots Section XX names (Kahneman and Tversky to Douglas and Duke; Kyle to Almgren-Chriss; Bachelier to Mandelbrot to Taleb; Kelly to Thorp to Tharp) to their modern descendants in the KB.
It collects the formulas of each field: Kyle's lambda and square-root impact (microstructure), standard error and SQN (inference), deflated Sharpe (overfitting), Kelly and ruin (risk).
Rule 1 sources ideas from academic and industry research (for example SSRN papers) and tells the trader to take the market behaviour a paper found, not to copy its exact recipe.

measurable_as: Microstructure: effective spread and slippage on one's own fills compared with quoted spread.
Behavioural finance: a disposition-effect test on one's own journal (holding time and exit rule adherence for losers versus winners).
Overfitting: deflated Sharpe ratio or PBO for each researched strategy.
Inference: confidence intervals on win rate and expectancy for each setup.
Risk: Monte Carlo probability of ruin and drawdown at the chosen risk fraction.
gaps: Madhavan's survey and Kahneman and Tversky's 1979 paper, both named in Section XX, have no linkable node in the allowed index.
The concept notes have no dedicated behavioural-finance entry for the disposition effect or overtrading research; it appears only inside the psychology note.
Of the backtest-overfitting literature only the deflated Sharpe paper is linkable; probability-of-backtest-overfitting and data-snooping papers are not nodes in the index.

nodes.summary: A first-person restatement of the whole philosophy as commitments: the market as an evolving relationship expressed through price, recurrence without guaranteed repetition, destinations as hypotheses, probability and mathematics as instruments for testing beliefs, agreement of understanding, evidence and maths before acting, stepping back, protecting capital and emotional discipline, keeping records, and never confusing confidence with knowledge or profit with proof.

grounded_in.why: The manifesto's 'seek an edge, test it, protect it through disciplined execution, and examine whether it remains valid' is the KB's edge lifecycle, including decay.
'Probability is central because certainty is unavailable' and judging decisions on more than profit or loss restate the probabilistic-thinking note.
'Price is the visible expression of interactions occurring within the market' is the microstructure view of price formation.
'Similar conditions may produce similar tendencies, yet each situation must be evaluated within its own context' is regime-conditional thinking.
Acting only when 'the probability, the potential reward, and the risk justify the action' is an expectancy condition.
'I will not risk my ability to continue trading' is the survival constraint of the risk-of-ruin note.
The commitments against fear, greed, frustration and the desire to recover losses are the psychology note's subject.
'I will maintain a record of my decisions, examine my mistakes, test my assumptions' is the journal-and-review loop.

supported_by.why: Douglas's probabilistic mindset and acceptance of risk before entry match the manifesto's commitments to process and to being wrong.
Duke's separation of decision quality and outcome supports 'I will not judge a decision solely by whether it produces a profit or a loss'.
Taleb's case that luck masquerades as skill is the independent argument behind 'I will not confuse profit with proof'.
Thorp's career, a measurable edge plus disciplined sizing plus risk control, is the manifesto's 'seek an edge, test it, protect it' lived out.
Livermore's lessons (the market is never wrong, cut losses, sit tight) support the manifesto's humility toward the market and patience in execution.
Dalio's practice of learning systematically from mistakes supports 'remain willing to change my understanding when the evidence demands it'.

challenged_by.why: The manifesto's 'I will not attempt to control the market' assumes the trader stands outside it; reflexivity says perceptions and actions of participants help create the outcomes they try to predict.
The belief that one can 'develop an increasingly accurate understanding' of the market's behaviour is challenged by evidence that, at many horizons, price changes are close to unpredictable.
Druckenmiller's case for concentrating heavily when conviction is high pulls against the manifesto's emphasis on patience and capital protection as the default.

operationalized_by.why: Its one-sentence version (a structurally motivated edge, traded only in its regime, sized to survive, executed without hesitation, audited relentlessly) is the manifesto in operational form.
It turns the manifesto's commitments (edge, context, invalidation, size, state of mind) into a scored gate with a no-trade threshold.
Its rule that there is no sudden breakthrough moment and one green month proves nothing echoes 'I will not confuse profit with proof', and staged sizing enacts patience.

measurable_as: Each manifesto commitment as a journal flag (for example 'traded without understanding', 'risked continuation'), tracked as a violation rate over time.
Proportion of trading days on which the trader stepped back, and the forward outcome of the skipped setups.
Whether profitable periods coincide with high adherence or with luck: compare adherence-weighted and unweighted expectancy.
Edge-validity checks: rolling out-of-sample expectancy per setup against its original estimate.
gaps: The KB has no reconciliation of the manifesto's 'humble understanding' with reflexivity or with concentration-when-confident practice; the tensions are only implicit across notes.
No KB tool turns the manifesto's commitments into a periodic self-audit beyond the pre-trade checklist.

nodes.summary: Position size must be set so that runs of unfavourable outcomes, which even a positive-expectancy strategy will produce, cannot needlessly threaten the trader's ability to keep participating.

grounded_in.why: The principle is a sizing rule; the note's fixed-fractional and volatility-unit models and 'size down in drawdowns' are its tools.
Streak damage 1 - (1 - f)^k, recovery asymmetry and the gambler's-ruin approximation are the mathematics of why size governs survival.
Kelly gives the growth-optimal fraction and shows that betting more than about twice Kelly produces negative growth even with an edge, an upper bound for 'protect capital'.
The note's rule that stop distance times size, not leverage, sets risk is the mechanism by which capital is protected.
Several correlated positions at small risk each are one larger bet, so protecting capital requires a portfolio-heat cap as well as a per-trade cap.
Treating the drawdown limit as the bankroll and using daily loss limits are concrete forms of sizing so unfavourable sequences do not end the account.
The principle exists because a positive expectancy only pays off over many trades, which requires surviving the losing streaks along the way.
Sizing inversely to volatility (the Turtle N unit) keeps the money at risk constant as market conditions change.

supported_by.why: Tharp's position-sizing strategies, SQN and R-multiple simulation show how size, not entry, decides whether objectives are met without ruin.
Vince shows that leverage drives both growth and ruin, the formal basis for sizing to survive.
Kelly's growth-optimal betting fraction is the original mathematical link between edge, bet size and long-run survival.
The collected work on fractional Kelly explains why practitioners bet a fraction of the growth-optimal size to cut drawdowns.
Feller's classic treatment of ruin problems is the probability theory behind 'unfavourable sequences can end participation'.
Hite's risk-first rule of never risking more than about 1% on a trade is a practitioner statement of the principle.
Jones's emphasis on defence first and sizing down when trading poorly (documented in Market Wizards) independently argue capital protection.
LTCM's collapse shows leverage, correlation and liquidity risk overwhelming a strong model, a case study in what the principle prevents.

challenged_by.why: Druckenmiller's argument for concentration and Soros doubling the sterling short show that some of the largest documented gains came from sizing far above survival-first norms when conviction was high.
Stops do not guarantee the maximum loss in gaps and limit moves, and correlations rise toward one in crises, so sizing from stop distance can understate how much a single sequence can take.
Gunther's axiom to always bet meaningfully argues that very small fractions protect capital at the cost of never compounding it, a tension the principle does not address.

operationalized_by.why: Rule 8 sizes each position so a stopped-out trade costs only 0.5 to 1% of total equity, and rule 13 adds exposure only as trades work and the market confirms.
Both models risk 0.25 to 0.5% of the account per trade with a stop that is never widened.
Rule 10 allocates 5 to 25% of the account per strategy with an average loss of about 0.5% of that allocation, sizes by risk of ruin, and rule 12 cuts size when drawdown nears its Monte Carlo maximum.
Rule 8 grades a trade before sizing it and caps risk at 80%, 30%, 15% or 5% of the daily stop for A+, A, B and C trades.
Rule 14 ends the day after two losses, a hard circuit breaker on losing sequences.
Its L6 block gives fixed-fractional size, streak damage, recovery after drawdown and the gambler's-ruin approximation.

measurable_as: Monte Carlo shuffle and resampling of the journal's R-multiples at candidate risk fractions: probability of a 20% or 50% drawdown and of breaching a ruin threshold.
Realised maximum drawdown and longest losing streak compared with the simulated distribution.
Realised loss divided by planned loss per trade, to measure slippage through stops and gaps.
Total open risk including correlated positions (portfolio heat) at each point in time.
Chosen risk fraction compared with an estimated Kelly fraction, with the estimate's uncertainty.
gaps: Most Chart Fanatics playbooks leave risk per trade and daily or weekly limits 'not specified' (for example Gala Trades, Marci Silfrain, Clement Ang, Jared Tendler), so the KB has few concrete T2 sizing rules to test.
There is no KB data on how often and by how much stops are gapped through by instrument.
No KB guidance on shrinking size to reflect uncertainty in the edge estimate, beyond the fractional-Kelly heuristic.
Portfolio-level drawdown caps across several strategies are not specified anywhere (the Naoufel Taief note lists this as missing).

nodes.summary: Fear, greed, frustration and the urge to win back losses must not override the tested process, and the method should be revised only through evidence from disciplined investigation, never through emotional impulse.

grounded_in.why: The note covers loss aversion, revenge trading, FOMO and tilt, the emotions the principle names, and lists operational guardrails against them.
Thinking in distributions removes the emotional weight of a single loss, which is Douglas's route to executing without fear.
Psychology rules written into the plan (maximum trades, a break after N losses, no revenge trades) make the process the decision-maker.
Emotion tags and rule-adherence flags in the journal are how emotional interference is detected and separated from method problems.
Oversized positions amplify emotion, so sizing is a practical lever for emotional independence.
Pre-set daily loss limits and size cuts after a drawdown stop frustration from turning losses into a demand for recovery.

supported_by.why: Douglas argues that fear is a misperception of risk and that a loss accepted before entry leaves nothing to fear in the moment.
Douglas's earlier book argues that mental frameworks about risk and being wrong are the bottleneck, not analysis.
Tendler diagnoses greed, fear, tilt and discipline problems and fixes their underlying flaws, a method for the principle.
Hougaard argues that the edge is behavioural and that traders must train against instinct, cutting losses instantly and without drama.
Kahneman's loss aversion and prospect theory explain why traders hold losers and cut winners, the bias the principle is meant to override.
Steenbarger's self-coaching lessons give structured ways to keep emotional states from steering decisions.

challenged_by.why: Coates finds that hormones such as testosterone and cortisol drive cycles of risk-taking, so emotional states are partly physiological and may need external limits rather than willpower alone.
Profit targets, trailing drawdowns and deadlines in the prop-firm environment most KB traders use push toward over-aggression, creating the emotional pressure the principle tries to remove.

operationalized_by.why: Rule 8's mid-session reset (name the emotion, move, refocus, then at most one small trade or a 15-minute break, with the session over if that limit is broken) and rule 9's emotional expected value are direct procedures for the principle.
Rule 14 ends the day after two losses, which the note links to stopping revenge trading.
