Rule 27 allows about three attempts per ticker and then stops trading the name, an explicit tilt control.
Rule 13 hides the running P&L and manages from the chart, and the comfort test treats a loss you would not be at ease taking as a sign of oversizing.
Its rule that emotions taking over means the size is too big turns emotional interference into a sizing signal.
Item 10 requires no revenge, no FOMO and no tilt, and that the trade's loss be accepted in advance.

measurable_as: Expectancy and rule adherence of trades tagged calm versus trades tagged fear, FOMO, frustration or revenge in the journal.
Trade frequency and size in the trades after a loss or a losing streak compared with baseline, as a revenge-trading signature.
Disposition-effect test: holding time of losers versus winners relative to the plan, and early exits before target.
Rule changes made within a few days of a drawdown versus changes made at a scheduled review.
Compliance rate with session-stop rules.
gaps: No KB data links emotion tags to performance; the psychology frameworks are practitioner heuristics (Tendler's 60/80/100% scale has no scoring method).
The KB has no operational test of when a method change is evidence-based rather than impulsive (for example a minimum sample or review cadence before a rule changes).
Behavioural-finance papers on the disposition effect and overtrading are not linkable nodes in the index.

nodes.summary: Keep a journal of hypotheses, decisions, outcomes and changes in understanding, and let the accumulated record, not memory, improve future decisions.

grounded_in.why: The principle names the journal; the note supplies its fields and its daily, weekly and monthly review cadence, including an edge-decay check.
Accumulated evidence becomes useful through per-setup metrics such as expectancy, profit factor and SQN.
The record is what lets expectancy be estimated per setup rather than assumed.
Investigating why results differ requires a regime label on each record.
Recorded decisions are judged against the written plan, and changes in understanding become plan revisions.
Comparing live records with backtest expectations is how the journal detects decay or execution problems.
Letting evidence accumulate over many trades, rather than reacting to one, is the probabilistic stance the principle requires.

supported_by.why: Soros's real-time diary of hypotheses and changes of mind is a published record-and-investigate practice.
Brandt's trade logs and the analysis of why most signals fail show a professional record used to investigate a method.
Dalio's systematic recording of mistakes and lessons is an independent case for turning experience into examinable records.
Steenbarger's self-coaching is built on reviewing one's own trading records.
Duke argues for reviewing decisions in a way that separates skill from luck, which needs a record of the reasoning at the time.
Davey's process includes monitoring live systems against their development results, record-and-investigate applied to systems.

challenged_by.why: Mining the journal for patterns after the fact is itself a multiple-testing exercise, so 'accumulated evidence' can produce false lessons unless the questions are fixed in advance.
If edges evolve with the market's ecology, older records describe conditions that may no longer exist, so a longer record is not automatically better evidence for the next decision.

operationalized_by.why: Its development loop logs mistakes for a week, picks the most important one, finds the root cause with five whys, writes a measurable fix and treats friction as the next data point.
Stage 2 collects win rate, per-setup and time-of-day data with daily review, and Stage 4 uses journal data only for small refinements while tracking week-over-week consistency.
Its review rule tracks performance by setup grade.
Rule 11 monitors live results against Monte Carlo ranges and treats a breach as a reason to review, not as automatic proof the strategy is broken.
Its L8 stage journals per setup, regime and session and compares live results with the backtest.

measurable_as: Journal completeness: share of trades, and of no-trade decisions, with every pre-trade field filled.
Learning curve: rolling expectancy and adherence rate before and after each documented rule change (interrupted time series).
Frequency of a targeted mistake before and after a root-cause fix.
Monthly gap between live and backtest expectancy per setup.
Hypothesis log: number of hypotheses revised or retired, and the evidence that triggered each change.
gaps: The KB gives no statistical method for journal review (minimum sample per slice, control for multiple comparisons).
There is no standard taxonomy of trading mistakes to make records comparable over time.
The full journal template in 00_philosophy has no node id, so the principle cannot be linked to it in the graph.

nodes.summary: The pull of profit must never replace checking whether a trade is justified: understanding, evidence, a tested model, probabilities, the cost of being wrong and fit with the process come first, and the money is judged only afterwards.

grounded_in.why: The principle targets the emotional attraction of money, which the psychology note links to over-trading, FOMO and ignoring stops.
'Does this decision follow my established process?' presupposes a written plan.
Judging the process rather than a single trade's payoff is the probabilistic-thinking stance against 'resulting'.
Money is properly evaluated as expectancy over many trades, not as what one trade might pay.
The principle says to follow the process that has demonstrated an advantage, which is an edge in the KB's sense.
Expressing outcomes in R rather than currency is a practical way to take money out of the decision.

supported_by.why: Duke's warning against judging decisions by their outcomes is the independent argument for process before money.
Douglas argues that consistency comes from executing a defined edge without fixation on any single trade's result.
Taleb shows that profits can come from luck, so money cannot by itself show that a decision was justified.
Tharp's R-multiples measure every trade in units of initial risk, shifting attention from money to the system's expectancy.
Faith reports that Turtles who failed usually did so by not taking every signal, showing that departures from process, not the rules, destroyed results.

challenged_by.why: Prop-firm economics put money targets, payouts and consistency rules at the centre of most KB traders' environment; JJ Simon's playbook even sets stops and targets from the account model rather than chart invalidation, which makes money-first decisions structural.

operationalized_by.why: Rule 1 states that the goal is not to make a dollar figure but to build a repeatable process, with money as a by-product.
Rule 13 hides the running P&L and manages from the chart, and rule 17 grades the process rather than the P&L.
Rule 9 runs strategies with no discretionary overrides and rule 12 forbids pulling a strategy for short-term underperformance, a 'process over prediction' design.
Setup B states that the goal is consistency, not catching every move, and the method is judged by overall profit factor rather than single trades.
None of its ten gates concerns the profit amount; a trade proceeds only if at least seven are met.

measurable_as: Share of trades that were unplanned or below the checklist threshold, and their expectancy versus planned trades.
Size and frequency changes after large wins or losses, as a money-salience effect.
Session outcomes with the P&L display hidden versus visible.
Days on which trading continued to reach a money target, and the R of trades taken after the target pressure began.
Forward outcomes of setups skipped because the process did not justify them.
gaps: The KB has no evidence on how payout or profit-target incentives change trader behaviour.
Research on overtrading and the cost of trading activity (for example Barber and Odean) is not a linkable node in the index.
No KB comparison exists between process grades and P&L for any strategy.

nodes.summary: Which market behaviours are genuinely repeatable, given that some patterns in historical data arise by chance and reflect no lasting relationship?

grounded_in.why: A repeatable behaviour that pays after costs is the KB's definition of an edge.
The note sets out the efficient-markets null and the counter-evidence (momentum, short-horizon reversal, variance-ratio tests) that bears on repeatability.
Separating repeatable behaviour from chance patterns is the multiple-testing problem.
Almost every pattern claim is a claim about autocorrelation structure, which these tools test.
Time-series momentum, documented across a long history of futures data, is one of the KB's strongest candidates for a repeatable behaviour.
Short-horizon mean reversion is the other main candidate the KB lists against the random-walk null.
Repeatability can only be established by testing defined rules on history and then on new data.

supported_by.why: Lo and MacKinlay's variance-ratio tests reject the random walk and find predictable components, evidence that some behaviours recur.
Aronson shows that most technical rules fail rigorous, data-snooping-aware testing, so repeatability must be demonstrated rather than assumed.
Ilmanen synthesises the evidence on value, carry, momentum and volatility premia, the most studied candidates for repeatable behaviour.
Bulkowski reports statistics on chart-pattern failure rates and average moves, a measured rather than anecdotal view of repeatability.
The econometrics text covers formal tests of return predictability, the tools for this question.
Asness's factor and time-series momentum research is a body of evidence on behaviours that have persisted across markets.
Lo argues that edges appear, get crowded and decay, so repeatability is real but conditional and temporary.

challenged_by.why: Malkiel's case for efficiency implies that for most traders and horizons the honest answer may be that almost no visible pattern is exploitable.
If participants' beliefs and actions change the market, a behaviour's repeatability is not fixed: discovering and trading it can alter or end it.

operationalized_by.why: It treats four candidate behaviours (opening-range breakout, VWAP trend, post-earnings drift, overnight anomaly) as hypotheses tied to a stated cause and tested under the same out-of-sample protocol.
It generates thousands of rule sets and keeps only the few that survive robustness tests across parameters, regimes, markets and timeframes.
It restricts the search to three directional behaviours (short-term momentum, mean reversion, long-term momentum) and tells the trader to research each market's thresholds.
The expected best Sharpe from N skill-less trials and the Hurst exponent give quantitative tests of chance versus structure.
It shows most 'new' strategies re-express six to eight old ideas, narrowing the candidates for repeatable behaviour to those with long histories.

measurable_as: Out-of-sample persistence of a defined behaviour's conditional frequency, tested against a null corrected for multiple testing.
Variance-ratio, autocorrelation and Hurst estimates by horizon and market.
Replication rate of a behaviour across markets and non-overlapping periods.
Placebo test: the same rule on shuffled or simulated random-walk data, to estimate how often it 'works' by chance.
gaps: The KB has no catalogue of independently replicated market behaviours with effect sizes.
Practitioner playbooks rarely give a sample size or win rate, so their behaviours cannot be checked for repeatability.
The evidence lab found only 1 of 11 in-sample conditional differences holding out of sample, on a handful of markets; broader evidence is missing.

nodes.summary: How can the conditions a probability estimate depends on (volatility, trend, liquidity and others) be defined so they are measurable and identified the same way every time?

grounded_in.why: The regime note's trend/range by high/low volatility grid and its detectors are the KB's starting vocabulary for conditions.
Realised volatility, ATR and implied volatility are the measurable forms of the volatility condition Section XIX names.
The Hurst exponent, variance ratio and structural-break tests are quantitative regime diagnostics.
Balance versus imbalance is a condition definition used by several playbooks.
Clean higher highs and higher lows versus overlapping swings is the structural definition of trend versus range.
Liquidity is one of the conditions Section XIX names and must be measured, for example by depth or volume.
Time of day is the most easily measured condition many playbooks rely on.
Labelling and feature construction (including structural-break features) are the formal way to turn conditions into data.

supported_by.why: Hamilton's regime-switching models are the standard statistical way to define and estimate market states.
Tsay's GARCH and volatility models make the volatility condition measurable and forecastable.
Kaufman's reference includes measures such as the efficiency ratio and testing methods for regime filters.
Dalton defines day types and balance versus imbalance, a discretionary but explicit taxonomy of conditions.
Wilder introduced ATR and ADX, two of the most used numeric measures of volatility and trend strength.
López de Prado covers structural-break features and event sampling, ways to define conditions in data.

challenged_by.why: Every extra condition splits the sample further and adds another way to overfit, so more precise conditions can make estimates less reliable, not more.
Its discretionary-versus-systematic conflict shows that many practitioners define conditions by judgment, which may not be reducible to consistent measurements.

operationalized_by.why: Rule 2 requires the 5, 9, 13 (or 15) and 21 EMAs to be clearly stacked in the trade direction and marks the setup invalid if they cross or tangle, a numeric regime gate.
Market state (balanced or out of balance) is the first gate and selects which of two models applies.
Rule 8's Three-Loss Rule uses three failed reversions in a session as an observable sign that the market is trending and setting a new fair value.
Rules 4 and 6 define 'normal' movement and 'abnormal' deviation numerically (average daily range versus a 2x expansion; usual distance from a 5-day SMA versus a much larger gap).
It gives the Hurst exponent and Wilder's ATR formula as measurable regime inputs.

measurable_as: Agreement (for example Cohen's kappa) between two people, or the same person on two dates, labelling the same charts.
Stability of labels under small parameter changes (for example an ADX threshold of 20 versus 25).
Real-time versus hindsight labels: classify with frozen cut-offs as the data arrive and compare with labels assigned later.
Observations per condition cell, against a minimum sample.
Whether the label changes the out-of-sample distribution of outcomes (for example a two-sample KS test).
gaps: Many playbooks list the key condition as unspecified, for example an objective test for balance (Fabio Valentini), what a healthy market is (Ariel Hernandez) and expanded versus dead volatility (Dhesi).
The KB has no standard regime taxonomy with numeric thresholds shared across notes.
There is no guidance on testing the reliability of discretionary condition labels.

nodes.summary: How reliable are probability estimates when a historical success rate may rest on too few observations or on conditions that will not recur?

grounded_in.why: The note warns that a win rate estimated from 30 trades has a wide confidence interval and should be treated as a belief to update.
Sample means and variances converge slowly under fat tails, and the note recommends Bayesian updating of edge estimates.
SQN is essentially a t-statistic of the edge, a direct measure of how distinguishable the estimate is from zero.
The quantity whose reliability matters is expectancy, which combines win rate and payoff estimates.
Selection among many variants biases the chosen estimate upward, a main source of unreliability.
The Kelly note shows that overestimating the edge leads to overbetting, so estimate reliability feeds directly into sizing.

supported_by.why: Wasserman covers confidence intervals and the bootstrap, the tools for stating how reliable an estimate is.
Casella and Berger give the theory of estimation and its uncertainty.
Blitzstein and Hwang teach conditioning and expectation, the basis for estimating probabilities under defined conditions.
Taleb shows that under fat tails the law of large numbers works slowly, so historical frequencies are less reliable than standard formulas suggest.
The deflated Sharpe ratio quantifies how selection from many trials inflates an estimate.
Taleb's survivorship-bias argument explains why a good historical record can be a poor guide to future frequency.

challenged_by.why: Jaynes treats probability as a degree of belief updated by evidence, which reframes the philosophy's frequency-based question ('how frequently have they occurred') as one about posterior uncertainty rather than a single success rate.
If the market's ecology keeps changing, there may be no stable underlying probability for a large sample to converge on, so reliability is limited by non-stationarity, not only by sample size.

operationalized_by.why: It gives the standard error of an estimated win rate (about plus or minus 7 points at n = 50 and p = 0.5) and SQN as a t-statistic.
Item 1 requires at least 30 logged instances with positive expectancy after costs before a setup counts as an edge.
It suggests about 50 evaluation backtests to reduce small-sample noise in the pass-rate estimate.
Rule 8 resamples trades with replacement to estimate the range of expected return, drawdown, longest losing streak and the chance of a given loss.
Rule 7 makes Monte Carlo drawdown, not backtest drawdown, the basis for setting expectations.

measurable_as: Confidence or credible intervals on win rate and expectancy per setup, and the sample needed for a target precision or power.
Calibration of stated probabilities against realised frequencies on new data (Brier score).
Selection haircut: the gap between in-sample estimates of chosen rules and their out-of-sample results.
Bootstrap probability that expectancy is zero or below.
Stability of the estimate across non-overlapping sub-periods.
gaps: The KB has no calibration tools (Brier score, reliability diagrams) for checking probability estimates.
No concept note turns an edge size into the number of trades needed to detect it; the evidence lab's power calculation has no node id.
Practitioner win-rate claims rarely state a sample size, so their reliability cannot be assessed.

nodes.summary: Do spreads, commissions, slippage, financing and execution conditions leave a positive expectancy, or do they turn an apparently profitable strategy into a losing one?

grounded_in.why: The note covers implementation shortfall, temporary and permanent impact and the square-root law, the mechanics of execution cost.
It lists spread, commission, slippage against intended price and missed fills as the costs to log.
The bid-ask spread and order types that create costs are microstructure.
Thin liquidity widens spreads and slippage, so the cost question depends on the liquidity of the market and session.
The scalping note says costs are a large share of each target, making cost survival the deciding test for short-horizon edges.
The question is whether expectancy stays positive once costs are subtracted, as the philosophy's EV formula requires.
Realistic costs, especially slippage on stops and around news, are one of the four requirements of a systematic backtest.

supported_by.why: Harris explains the components of the spread, how transaction costs are measured and why short-term trading is close to zero-sum after costs.
Bouchaud and co-authors document the square-root impact law, which says how costs grow with order size.
Almgren and Chriss model the trade-off between impact cost and price risk, the foundation of execution-cost analysis.
Kissell and Glantz cover transaction-cost analysis, the measurement this question needs.
Narang treats a transaction-cost model as one of the core parts of any quant strategy.
Johnson explains execution algorithms and order routing, the practical levers on cost.
Lewis describes how market structure and latency can disadvantage slower orders, a cost retail traders rarely measure.

challenged_by.why: Pedersen argues that inefficiencies persist because costs and limits to arbitrage deter others, so costs are not only an obstacle but the reason some edges exist, which makes the question one of relative cost advantage.

operationalized_by.why: Rule 2 requires the expected move per trade to be large next to fees, spread and slippage (its example: about 0.2% round-trip costs take half of a 0.4% edge), and rule 1 avoids the most competitive high-liquidity, low-timeframe mix.
Its risk section counts hard-to-borrow and locate fees as costs that eat profit and reuses located shares through recycling to reduce them.
It costs the prop route explicitly: a $100 evaluation passing 25% of the time costs about $400 per funded account, to be compared with expected payouts.
It gives per-trade friction as half the spread plus commission plus slippage, and the square-root impact formula.
It resolves the high-R:R versus high-win-rate conflict with the rule that only expectancy after costs matters.

measurable_as: Break-even cost per side: the cost at which net expectancy reaches zero, compared with measured spread plus commission.
Implementation shortfall per trade from the journal: fill price versus decision price, and the distribution of slippage on stops.
Net expectancy with confidence intervals by market and timeframe, and the ratio of cost to gross edge.
Sensitivity of out-of-sample results to 1x, 2x and 3x the assumed costs.
Turnover times cost per trade compared with gross expectancy per period.
gaps: The KB has no measured spread or slippage data by instrument or session.
Both systematic frameworks (Matteo Conti, Naoufel Taief) leave cost and slippage assumptions unspecified, and the evidence lab uses flat cost assumptions.
Financing and borrow costs appear only in the Kris Verma note; overnight financing for leveraged FX and futures is not covered.

nodes.summary: Does a relationship that worked in one period keep working when market conditions change, or does it weaken or disappear?

grounded_in.why: The note says the same setup can have opposite expectancy in different regimes, which is exactly this question.
Its adaptive-markets synthesis says edges appear, get crowded and decay, a mechanism for relationships weakening.
Structural-break tests and rolling estimates are the statistical way to detect when a relationship has changed.
The edge note warns that edges decay as they are crowded and must be monitored.
Volatility clustering and regime shifts change stop distances, targets and the behaviour of setups.
Walk-forward testing evaluates a strategy only on forward segments, a direct test of survival across periods.
Its monthly or quarterly edge-decay check against backtest expectations is the live monitor for this question.

supported_by.why: Lo's hypothesis that efficiency changes with the ecology of participants explains why relationships weaken over time.
Hamilton's regime-switching models give a formal treatment of relationships that change between states.
Marks shows how economic, credit and psychological cycles change the environment in which any strategy operates.
LTCM's models, built on one set of conditions, failed when correlations and liquidity changed, a case study of failure under regime change.
Carver's emphasis on robust, simple rules and avoiding overfitting is aimed at strategies that survive changing conditions.
Davey's development process includes monitoring live systems for deterioration after deployment.

challenged_by.why: Covel's case that price-based trend following with strict risk control is durable and even crisis-resilient suggests some slow, diversified relationships do survive regime change, so the answer may differ sharply by strategy type.
If regime breaks are rare, high-impact events that are systematically underestimated, survival can often be judged only after the fact, which limits how far the question can be answered in advance.

operationalized_by.why: Rule 7 requires in-sample and out-of-sample periods to include different regimes (bull, bear, high and low volatility), and rules 11 to 13 keep an incubation pool, bench strategies near their expected maximum drawdown and replace them.
Rule 2 ties each model to a cause so the trader can notice when it stops applying, and rule 11 reviews a strategy when live results leave the Monte Carlo range.
Rules 8 and 9 stop reversion trades after three failures in a session and drop an old fair price once value has clearly moved.
Rule 12 treats research as continuous because edges decay as more capital trades them, fastest on lower timeframes.
It runs separate trend and mean-reversion models selected by market state, so a regime change switches the model instead of breaking it.
Stage 5 tracks performance across market conditions so the trader can adapt.

measurable_as: Rolling-window expectancy of the strategy's R series with structural-break tests (Chow, CUSUM).
Performance by regime bucket with cut-offs frozen in sample, and whether the sign of expectancy holds in each bucket.
Walk-forward efficiency: out-of-sample over in-sample performance per window.
Share of time live drawdown spends outside the Monte Carlo percentile bands.
Performance before and after a behaviour became widely published.
gaps: No Chart Fanatics strategy in the KB has a multi-regime test record.
There is no standard decay metric or benching threshold in the KB; the Naoufel Taief note itself leaves 'extended underperformance' undefined.
The adaptive-markets and post-publication-decay papers are not linkable nodes in the index; only Lo's book is.

nodes.summary: Can the trader carry out a sound strategy consistently, or will emotional decisions, inconsistent execution or excess risk undermine it?

grounded_in.why: Emotional decisions are the first failure mode Section XIX names, the subject of the psychology note.
Consistency means doing what the written plan says, trade after trade.
Inconsistent triggers, order types and fills are the execution side of the question.
The note warns that skipping trades after losses destroys the sample the edge depends on.
Rule-adherence flags are how execution consistency is measured.
Excessive risk, the third failure mode named, is a sizing problem.
The note warns that strategies behave differently on evaluation and live accounts because fills, size and psychology change.

supported_by.why: Faith reports that the Turtles who failed mostly did so by not taking every signal, a direct case of sound rules undone by inconsistent execution.
Covel's history of what happened to the Turtles shows the same rules producing very different results across traders.
Douglas's principles (act without hesitation, never violate the rules) and his 20-trade exercise target consistent execution of a defined edge.
Hougaard argues most traders know the rules but few execute them because the brain resists, so the edge is behavioural.
Tendler treats discipline lapses as emotional problems with diagnosable root causes.
Schwager's interviewees share discipline and risk control as the common factor behind very different methods.

challenged_by.why: Its discretionary-versus-systematic conflict, resolved through automation or meta-labeling, suggests consistency can be engineered by removing discretion rather than achieved by the trader's discipline.
Coates's physiology of risk-taking implies that a trader's risk appetite shifts with winning and losing streaks, so perfect consistency may be biologically limited.

operationalized_by.why: Rule 9 exports and runs each strategy automatically with no discretionary overrides.
Stage 3 cuts every trade outside the plan, even ones that work, and Stage 4 tracks consistency week over week, judging execution rather than outcome.
Its loop turns each repeated mistake into a specific, measurable fix and rejects vague resolutions to be more disciplined as a fix.
Rules 5 to 8 set a pre-session state check with one process goal, note emotional shifts during the session and use a reset with a hard session-ending limit.
Rules 6 and 9 use a fixed 10-point NQ stop, skip any setup that cannot take it cleanly, and name overtrading as the main danger.
A scored checklist applied before every trade standardises the decision so it is made the same way each time.

measurable_as: Signal capture rate: share of valid setups (found by replaying the written rules) that were actually taken live.
Deviation from plan: entry and exit slippage against plan, stop moves and early exits per trade.
Live versus backtest expectancy gap split into missed trades, slippage and rule violations.
Variance of risk per trade against the planned risk.
Behaviour after losses compared with baseline (trade frequency, size, setup grade).
gaps: The KB has no data on any trader's live-versus-backtest execution gap.
There is no KB definition or threshold for 'consistent' execution.
No KB evidence compares discretionary and automated execution of the same rules.

extension_candidates.title: Monte Carlo ranges as the line between normal variance and a broken edge
extension_candidates.idea: The philosophy asks whether a losing run is consistent with expected performance but gives no method. The KB's systematic playbooks shuffle and resample the trade list to get percentile bands for drawdown and losing streaks, treat a live breach as a trigger for review rather than proof of failure, bench rather than delete a strategy, and keep an incubation pool of replacements.

extension_candidates.title: Count the trials, then deflate the result
extension_candidates.idea: Section XVII warns against adjusting rules until they fit the past, but it does not say that the number of variants tried must be recorded and used to discount the winner. The KB adds the expected best Sharpe from N skill-less trials, the deflated Sharpe ratio and data-snooping-robust tests, which imply keeping a research log of every variant alongside the trading journal.

extension_candidates.title: Edges decay because they are found and crowded
extension_candidates.idea: The philosophy says a relationship may weaken in another period; the KB supplies a mechanism. Under the adaptive-markets view, edges attract capital and decay, lower-timeframe edges decay fastest, and a stated cause for each edge helps the trader see when it stops applying. This points to choosing less competitive markets and timeframes and to a scheduled decay check.

extension_candidates.title: Emotion as a state to manage, not only an interference to exclude
extension_candidates.idea: Principle 10 frames emotions as forces to keep out of decisions. The KB's psychology sources say some emotional energy is needed for performance (aim for the middle of an inverted U), that yesterday's frustration carries over as risk, that the expected value of another trade falls when one's state is poor, and that hormones shift risk appetite. They also treat an emotional takeover as a sign the position is too large. The remedy becomes structural: state checks, resets, session stops and size.

extension_candidates.title: A ceiling as well as a floor on size: Kelly and grade-based risk budgets
extension_candidates.idea: Section XIV and Principle 9 only guard against sizing too large. The KB adds that betting above about twice the Kelly fraction gives negative growth even with an edge, that fractional Kelly keeps most of the growth for far less drawdown, that size should be cut when the edge estimate is uncertain, and that a daily risk budget can be allocated by setup grade (A+, A, B, C).

extension_candidates.title: Protect capital at the portfolio level: correlation and uncorrelated strategies
extension_candidates.idea: The philosophy reasons about one strategy's sequence of trades. The KB adds that correlated positions at small risk each add up to one large bet, that correlations rise toward one in crises, and that a portfolio of three or four, or more, uncorrelated strategies can cut risk without cutting return. Capital preservation then needs a portfolio-heat cap and correlation limits.

extension_candidates.title: Fat tails limit what samples and stops can promise
extension_candidates.idea: The philosophy relies on the law of large numbers and on stop-defined risk. The KB adds that under fat tails sample means converge slowly, a historical Sharpe can rest on a few observations, high-win-rate strategies can hide tail risk, and stops do not guarantee the maximum loss in gaps. Estimates need wider uncertainty, and sizing should be set for the tail rather than the average loss.

extension_candidates.title: Review strengths and excursions, not only contradictions
extension_candidates.idea: Section XVI uses the journal mainly to expose wrong beliefs. The KB's review practice adds reviewing what one does well as carefully as mistakes (Steenbarger), logging MAE and MFE to tune stops and targets, and using a root-cause loop that fixes one recurring mistake at a time, risk mistakes first.

extensions.title: Name the counterparty
extensions.one_line: An explanation is defensible when it names who is on the other side and why; if no one can be named, assume adverse selection: you may be the one paying for someone else's information or urgency.

extensions.title: Shared models are part of the market, and stops are one of them
extensions.one_line: Section II's independence claim holds for a private model, but widely shared models (where crowds put stops, how they position) become liquidity that acts on the market, so invalidation at the obvious level can be run before the hypothesis is tested.

extensions.title: Observed interaction: a rung between price and inference
extensions.one_line: In central-book markets, aggressor side, delta, absorption (effort vs result) and Kyle's lambda add an observable 'interaction' step between price and interpretation, making some inferences testable while intent stays inferred.

extensions.title: Value is what the auction accepts
extensions.one_line: Section XV's value becomes operational in three senses (auction acceptance, event-defined fair price, anchored value), and limits to arbitrage explain why a known gap can persist.

extensions.title: Every edge is perishable
extensions.one_line: Under the adaptive-markets view, edges are found, crowded and decay (fastest on low timeframes in liquid markets), so each edge needs a stated cause, a re-validation schedule and a retirement rule.

extensions.title: Fat tails slow the law of large numbers
extensions.one_line: With power-law tails, sample means converge slowly, a few trades dominate a record, high-win-rate strategies hide tail risk and stops slip in gaps, so estimates need wider uncertainty and size must be set for the tail, not the average loss.

extensions.title: Count every trial, then deflate the winner
extensions.one_line: The best of N skill-less trials shows a Sharpe growing like sqrt(2 ln N), and finer conditions (Principle 4) multiply trials, so every variant must be logged and the winner judged by a deflated Sharpe or data-snooping test.

extensions.title: Start from a sceptical base rate, then score your calibration
extensions.one_line: Since most candidate patterns are noise, a new pattern should start near 'no edge' and be updated Bayesian-style, and the probabilities recorded in the journal should be checked for calibration.

extensions.title: A ready vocabulary of measurable conditions
extensions.one_line: The knowledge base already lists measurable regime detectors (trend/range x volatility, AMT balance and day type, Hurst, variance ratio, ATR percentile, EMA alignment, Bollinger environment, regime-switching models) that could become the philosophy's fixed default conditions.

extensions.title: Edges that need no story
extensions.one_line: Trend following enters because price is moving, names no destination and is among the best-documented anomalies, explained by risk premia or limits to arbitrage, so the philosophy must say whether a tested reason why a class of moves pays counts as understanding.

extensions.title: Costs are set by the relationship, not a constant
extensions.one_line: Section VII's flat cost term hides that spreads widen in fast markets, stops fill into thinning books, impact grows with the square root of size, and frequency multiplies costs, so costs must be estimated for the conditions actually traded and weighed against the expected move.

extensions.title: Expected value is not growth: size is part of the edge
extensions.one_line: An account compounds along one path at roughly mu - sigma^2/2, so positive EV is enough only at a suitable size: beyond about 2x Kelly the same edge shrinks capital, which makes Sections VII and XIV two halves of one result and argues for fractional Kelly under estimation error.

extensions.title: Graded conviction instead of trade / no trade
extensions.one_line: Practitioners size by evidence strength (Holden's grade-based share of the daily stop, confluence-based sizing, ensemble agreement, meta-labeling, Kelly), which would make Principles 5, 6 and 9 graded rather than binary, provided grades follow written criteria and are validated in the journal.

extensions.title: Correlation: of positions, of strategies, of trades
extensions.one_line: Correlated positions are one bet and correlations rise in crises, uncorrelated strategies add breadth, and clustered or overlapping trades shrink the effective sample, so capital preservation needs portfolio-heat and correlation limits and the LLN needs independent observations.

extensions.title: Record the trade's path, not only its verdict
extensions.one_line: Average win and loss are produced by management rules (breakeven, partials, trailing, time stops), so a setup must be tested together with its management, the journal must log MAE/MFE, and review should cover strengths and one root-caused mistake at a time.

extensions.title: Expected-range bands: normal variance or a broken edge
extensions.one_line: Shuffling and resampling the trade list gives drawdown and losing-streak bands to monitor live results against; a breach triggers a size cut and review, not a verdict, and failing strategies are benched and replaced from an incubation pool rather than deleted.

extensions.title: Emotion is a state to measure, with structural stops
extensions.one_line: Rather than interference to exclude, emotion is energy with an optimal middle, a measurable state with carryover, a signal that size is too large and partly physiology, so the process is protected by state checks, session stops and size limits set while calm.

extensions.title: Stepping back has a cost: define it in advance and log it
extensions.one_line: Skipping valid signals destroyed failed Turtles' distributions and waiting for confirmation costs edge, so 'unclear' should be a condition written before the session, watching limited to fixed windows, and skipped setups logged so the cost of waiting is measured.

rejected.reason: The why calls Wyckoff's accumulation-markup-distribution-markdown cycle the knowledge base's 'oldest' recurring storyline, but the KB says otherwise: the Wyckoff note lists derived_from: [concept_dow_theory], and the Dow Theory note (c. 1900-1902) says its three primary-trend phases 'anticipate Wyckoff and ICT's AMD'.

The playbook breaks out only the opening push by float band (30-35% on 1-2M floats, 20-25% on 5-10M floats); the fade is a single figure (about 24-26%, average risk about 7%) with no float split, so the claim that it quantifies the 'opening push, fade' separately for each float band is not in the note.

Section V does not rest on AMD: the note models every candle and session as the same three phases with an assumed 'manipulation' intent, which is the 'every new chapter reproduces the previous one' reading Section V (and Section IV on inferring intent) warns against, and the storyline lineage is already covered by the Wyckoff link and the Tanja playbook.

Section XIII does not rest on prop-firm evaluation rules; the note gives the point only as one table row ('Profit target encourages over-aggression near deadlines'), so it is at most an illustration, and filing it as a foundation misleads.

The cited finding ('methods differ wildly; risk control does not') is about trading methods, not about following decisions rather than money; it says nothing about the pursuit of money distorting judgment and could be attached equally to XII, XIV or any section.

The pass-rate and cost-per-funded-account calculation is a systematic expected-value check of whether the return justifies the risk, which Section XIII endorses, and XIII already says 'profitability remains the objective of a trading system', so the cited evidence does not challenge the section.

In Dhesi's playbook, rule 12 calls a breakeven-stopped runner a success because half the position was already trimmed at the first target ('the model delivered the base hit'), so it is an outcome-accounting rule for trade management and does not separate decision quality from outcome.

'I will not attempt to control the market' is a commitment not to force trades, not a claim that the trader stands outside the market (the manifesto opens by calling the market a relationship between participants), so the stated tension misreads the line; the real reflexivity tension is Section II's independence claim, which the whole-philosophy node already links.

The liquidity Section XIX names is market liquidity measured by depth or volume, but concept_liquidity is about SMC/ICT stop pools and sweeps; its first lines send that 'microstructure liquidity' sense to concept_market_microstructure, so the link points to the wrong meaning.

The why relies on thin liquidity widening spreads and slippage, but this note only covers where stop orders cluster and how sweeps work, with nothing on spreads or slippage; that sense of liquidity lives in concept_market_microstructure, which is already linked here.

The note's discretionary-vs-systematic row is about trading style, not how to define conditions, and it resolves the conflict with a systematic filter and sizing on top of discretionary setups (meta-labeling), which supports measurable conditions rather than challenging the need for them.

The $100 evaluation / 25% pass rate / $400 per funded account sum is about the economics of prop-firm access, not the spreads, commissions, slippage, financing and execution costs the question asks an edge to survive, so it only loosely puts this question into practice.

The backtesting note says nothing about conditioning, regimes or defined situations (it covers clean data, costs, look-ahead and out-of-sample tests), and the why's 'with realistic costs' belongs to Principle 5, so here the link is generic padding that fits any testing-related part equally well.

The evidence lab's S1 does not say the regime at A moved P(B) more than detour depth did: out of sample a 1-ATR detour cut P(B) by 13-17 points and a 3-ATR detour by 33-40, against a regime gap of 12 points (19 at 3 ATR), 10 of the 12 unconditional points were reproduced by the memoryless null, and the regime note itself contains no such finding.

Every detail in the why is in the note, but the five-whys loop diagnoses the trader's own execution errors (selling early, badly placed stops), not changes in market evidence on a live position, so it belongs with Principle 11 (record and investigate), and 'fix risk mistakes before exit mistakes' only echoes 'manage risk first' on the surface.

The note is about time-of-day volatility and liquidity windows used as a filter and says nothing about stepping back when understanding fails or about limiting screen time, so Section IX does not rest on it and the link is only loosely related.

Paul Tudor Jones's 'defence first, size down when trading poorly' is a response to one's own drawdown and belongs to Principle 9 (protect capital), not to Section IX's rule of not trading a market one does not understand; sizing down is not stepping aside.

'The wizards share risk control and discipline across very different methods' is generic padding that could be attached to any principle, and it says nothing specific about staying out when the evidence is unclear.

The warnings the why cites (every reversal looks like a sweep afterwards, and a pool can be run with continuation) appear only in the Pitfalls section of concept_liquidity (07_concepts/liquidity.md lines 60-63); the liquidity-sweep-reversal note has no such caveat and simply sets out the setup's rules, variants and lineage.

The note settles discretionary versus systematic with a hybrid: a discretionary setup plus a meta-labeled filter and sizing. It never mentions automation or execution consistency, and taking discretion out would be one way to answer whether the trader can execute consistently, not a challenge to the question.

The why describes an introductory text on conditioning and expectation as 'the basis for estimating probabilities under defined conditions', which fits Principle 4 and the question of how to define conditions, not how reliable a historical success rate is given small samples or unrepresentative data. Here it is generic padding.

The polarity is wrong. Bayesian posterior uncertainty is a way to answer 'how reliable is that estimate', not something that complicates the question, and the KB's own notes (probability-fat-tails, probabilistic-thinking) present Jaynes-style updating as the right frame for estimating edge.

Rule 7's Monte Carlo reshuffles the order of the same trade list to estimate drawdown and losing streaks, which leaves the win rate and expectancy unchanged. It therefore does not test whether a probability estimate rests on too few observations or represents future conditions. It belongs under Section XI, where the same rule is already linked.

Zhang's rule makes price the judge of non-price stories (narrative and fundamentals count only if price confirms them), which is the reverse of Section IV's point that a price move alone cannot establish its cause and needs more evidence, so it does not put Section IV's observation-versus-inference split into practice.

Pavel's rule 10 only says not to wait for price to turn before entering a mean-reversion pullback; that is about entry timing, not Section VIII's need for understanding, evidence and mathematics to agree, and the playbook's 'measurable cost in price and R:R' is not in the note (it says only that waiting 'gives up part of the edge'), so the challenge does not apply.

The ontology sorts the knowledge base's notes into layers (maths, mechanics, setups, sizing, psychology, review). It is not a model of the market system and it tests nothing against the market, so the why misdescribes it and it does not put Section II's system-versus-model testing into practice.

The lineage map traces where trading ideas came from (several of its roots, such as Kelly sizing and probability misjudgment, are not market behaviours at all) and offers no test or evidence of repeatability; equating an idea's age with a behaviour's persistence is the linker's own inference, not something the note says.
